chapters.title: The Challenge of the Future
chapters.sourcePressure: The opening chapter separates horizontal progress that copies known things from vertical progress that creates something new, then turns that split into a demand for definite future-building and reality-based contrarian truth.
chapters.coreMove: Distinguish creation from replication before judging whether a project can change the future.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating the chapter as a motivational slogan about innovation or as permission to sound contrarian.
mustNotDriftInto: startup inspiration without the 0-to-1 versus 1-to-n split

chapters.title: Party Like It's 1999
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter treats the dot-com crash as a real failure that produced an overlearned startup rulebook: move incrementally, stay flexible, copy competitors, and trust product over sales.
chapters.coreMove: Audit inherited caution to see when a once-useful rule is now shrinking the bet.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the crash into either reckless anti-caution or bland lessons-learned wisdom.

chapters.title: All Happy Companies Are Different
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter contrasts monopoly-created uniqueness with competitive sameness, arguing that direct rivalry erodes profits and narrows strategic imagination.
chapters.coreMove: Look for the structural difference that lets a company escape direct comparison.
chapters.commonMisread: Saying monopoly is always good or competition is always bad as a moral claim.

chapters.title: The Ideology of Competition
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter asks why competition keeps moral prestige even when rivalry consumes attention and pushes companies into imitation.
chapters.coreMove: Notice when rivalry has become the frame that decides what you can see.
chapters.commonMisread: Reducing the idea to avoiding competitors instead of showing how rivalry captures attention.

chapters.title: Last Mover Advantage
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter shifts from escaping competition to asking what kind of business value endures over time, warning against mistaking firstness or novelty for durable strength.
chapters.coreMove: Evaluate a company by the value it can keep earning after the first excitement fades.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning durability into generic patience or long-term thinking without business mechanics.

chapters.title: You Are Not a Lottery Ticket
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter pushes against luck-only explanations and argues that uncertainty is not the same as helplessness; planning still changes the odds and the path.
chapters.coreMove: Replace lottery-ticket thinking with a definite plan that can shape uncertain outcomes.
chapters.commonMisread: Pretending planning guarantees success or, on the other side, treating uncertainty as fatalism.

chapters.title: Follow the Money
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter introduces venture and power-law logic: a small number of outcomes dominate the economics, so averaging can hide what matters most.
chapters.coreMove: Read a field by the weight of its outliers instead of the comfort of its averages.
chapters.commonMisread: Using power-law language as an excuse for reckless extreme bets.

chapters.title: Secrets
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter argues that valuable opportunities often begin as real truths that remain undiscovered, ignored, or underbelieved by consensus.
chapters.coreMove: Search for a hidden truth that reality supports before consensus is ready to reward it.
chapters.commonMisread: Confusing secrets with conspiracy, edginess, or contrarian performance.
mustNotDriftInto: be different for its own sake

chapters.title: Foundations
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter treats the founding moment as unusually consequential because early roles, ownership, incentives, and relationships harden into the company shape.
chapters.coreMove: Design the beginning as if early structure will become expensive to change.
chapters.commonMisread: Reducing foundations to legal paperwork or startup housekeeping.

chapters.title: The Mechanics of Mafia
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter moves from structure to culture, arguing that intense companies need mission fit, loyalty, and close cooperation rather than generic professionalism or perks.
chapters.coreMove: Test culture by whether shared purpose and role fit lower friction under pressure.
chapters.commonMisread: Romanticizing startup culture as vibes, perks, or cultish intensity.

chapters.title: If You Build It, Will They Come?
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter rejects the fantasy that a strong product automatically reaches customers and treats distribution as a core business design problem.
chapters.coreMove: Design the path to the customer with the same seriousness as the product itself.
chapters.commonMisread: Collapsing distribution into generic marketing or hype.

chapters.title: Man and Machine
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter frames technology as complementing human work when machines and people do different jobs well, not as a simple replacement story.
chapters.coreMove: Split a workflow so computers handle pattern-heavy work and people handle judgment-rich calls.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the chapter into automation panic or technological cheerleading.

chapters.title: Seeing Green
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter diagnoses why ambitious clean-tech bets can fail when timing, scale, distribution, and business design do not fit the promise.
chapters.coreMove: Diagnose a technology bet through timing, scale, and business design before admiring its ambition.
chapters.commonMisread: Sneering at clean technology or treating failure as proof that the mission was foolish.

chapters.title: The Founder's Paradox
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter holds founder upside and founder instability together, showing how unusual intensity can create force and distort judgment at the same time.
chapters.coreMove: Evaluate founder intensity as both a creative asset and an organizational risk.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the founder into either a hero, villain, or pop-psychology type.
